identity.title: More RLHF, More Trust? On The Impact of Preference Alignment On Trustworthiness

problem.claim: The study asks how general-purpose preference alignment affects LLM trustworthiness across toxicity, stereotypical bias, machine ethics, truthfulness, and privacy.

gap.claim: The assumed effect of RLHF on trustworthiness had not been rigorously evaluated.

contributions.claim: It evaluates preference-aligned models across five trustworthiness verticals and reports that RLHF does not automatically guarantee trustworthiness, with reverse effects often observed.
It adapts efficient-influence-function data-attribution methods to RLHF and provides estimated attribution scores for individual trustworthiness benchmarks.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state an adaptation of efficient influence-function data attribution to the RLHF setting for analyzing fine-tuning-data influence on trustworthiness benchmarks.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that RLHF on human preferences does not automatically guarantee trustworthiness and that reverse effects are often observed.
The authors report feasibility of their adapted attribution approach by providing estimated attribution scores.

narrative_sequence.summary: Trustworthiness is presented as a key consideration alongside LLM cognitive performance.
RLHF is widely used for preference alignment, but its effect on trustworthiness is described as insufficiently evaluated.
The study examines general-purpose preference-aligned models across five trustworthiness verticals.
The authors report non-automatic and sometimes reverse trustworthiness effects, then introduce RLHF-oriented data attribution with estimated scores.

source_observation.claim: The abstract evaluates alignment across five distinct trustworthiness verticals and reports that preference alignment can produce reverse effects.

lessons.interpretation: A single aggregate alignment claim may conceal dimension-specific trade-offs.
lessons.application: Report alignment outcomes separately across relevant trustworthiness dimensions and explicitly flag regressions or reverse effects.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when a study has a narrowly defined trustworthiness target or a validated aggregate metric.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the models, datasets, baselines, evaluation protocols, or which verticals exhibited reverse effects.
The attribution scores' validation, quantitative results, and practical interpretation are not described.
The abstract does not establish that the proposed alignment approaches improve trustworthiness.
